$comment: England & Wales, Property Law / Real Property (personal property/chattels, distinct from Land Law's registered-land content) - conversion of goods and the 'ministerial act' defence for an auctioneer who redelivers unsold goods to their apparent owner. Fresh research this session. Both nodes are post-1977/2003 and fetched directly, no BAILII/pre-2009 access issue to route around for the main case (Marcq was found on Find Case Law directly despite predating 2009's usual UKSC/UKHL cutoff, since Find Case Law's Court of Appeal coverage runs further back than its UKHL coverage).

authorities.name: Torts (Interference with Goods) Act 1977, s.11
authorities.date_note: Enactment year. The text verified this session is the current in-force (revised) version, with no outstanding effects noted on the page.
authorities.proposition: Contributory negligence is no defence to conversion or intentional trespass to goods (s.11(1)). Receipt of goods by way of pledge is itself conversion, if delivery of the goods would be conversion (s.11(2)) - the provision considered, and distinguished on the facts, in Marcq below. Mere denial of title is not, by itself, conversion (s.11(3)).
authorities.verification_note: Fetched live and directly this session, independently re-fetched and re-confirmed a second time - both fetches consistent on s.11(1)-(3)'s exact text.

authorities.name: Marcq v Christie, Manson & Woods Ltd
authorities.judge_or_panel: Peter Gibson LJ, Tuckey LJ (lead judgment), Keene LJ
authorities.proposition: An auctioneer who receives goods from their apparent (but not true) owner and simply redelivers them, unsold, to that same person, acts only 'ministerially' and is not liable in conversion, provided the auctioneer acted in good faith and without notice of any adverse claim - the auctioneer has merely changed the position of the goods, not the property in them. Separately, no bailor/bailee relationship arises between the auctioneer and the true owner where the auctioneer had no knowledge of that owner's interest and dealt only with the apparent owner. The court also considered and rejected an argument that the auctioneer's contractual lien/right-of-sale clause made its receipt of the goods a 'pledge' triggering conversion under TIGA 1977 s.11(2) - accepting s.11(2) as correctly stated but finding the contractual right of sale had never actually arisen on the facts.
authorities.verification_note: Fetched live and directly from Find Case Law this session, independently re-fetched and re-confirmed a second time - both fetches consistent on paragraph 24's 'ministerial act' holding. The case's own para 13 attributes the general threefold definition of conversion to Kuwait Airways Corp v Iraqi Airways Co, citing it as '[2002] UKHL 9' - independent search indicates the correct citation is actually [2002] UKHL 19 (Nos 4 and 5), a likely digit-drop in Marcq's own citation, not independently re-verified against the Kuwait Airways judgment itself (BAILII, parliament.uk, and vLex all blocked automated access this session). This does not affect Marcq's own holding, which is independently primary-verified regardless of whether its citation of Kuwait Airways is exact.

edges.verified_via: Marcq v Christie, Manson & Woods Ltd [2003] EWCA Civ 731, paras 9-10, fetched directly from Find Case Law and independently re-confirmed: accepts TIGA 1977 s.11(2) as a correct statement of law but distinguishes it on the facts, since the auctioneer's contractual right of sale had never actually arisen.

what_this_is_not: Two verified nodes covering one narrow point: an auctioneer's ministerial-act defence to conversion and the related no-bailment-without-knowledge rule. Does not cover the general elements of conversion in full (only referenced via Marcq's own citation of Kuwait Airways, itself flagged as not independently primary-verified), possession as against a wrongdoer, finders' rights, bailment generally, or any other Property Law / Real Property subject - all remain unbuilt.
